newsitem.title: USA: CBOT says corn/soy delivery plan legal, necessary.
newsitem.headline: CBOT says corn/soy delivery plan legal, necessary.

text.p: Chicago Board of Trade president Thomas Donovan said the exchange's proposed changes to delivery terms for its corn and soybean contracts were legal, necessary and should be approved without delay.

In a 37-page letter to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which is now weighing the proposed changes in an extended public comment period, Donovan outlined the Board's arguments for eliminating Toledo and St Louis as delivery points and switching to delivery points on the Illinois River.
"Under the applicable legal standard, the Board of Trade's proposed new delivery specifications should be approved without further delay," Donovan said.

Donovan cited the following arguments in support: --The Commodity Exchange Act only establishes a floor for what an exchange must do on grain delivery. The Act says delivery terms must tend to prevent or diminish market manipulation. CFTC cannot require the exchange to choose one delivery area over another as long as the proposed area tends to diminish manipulative activity, which it does, he said. --CFTC authority to order new delivery specifications is limited by statute. CFTC can only change such specifications when they do not accomplish the objectives of the Act. --In December 1996, CFTC suggested that CBOT drop Toledo as a delivery point, citing a letter to the exchange from CFTC that included four alternative delivery systems including cash settlements or delivery only at export points on the lower Mississippi River. --Donovan said "a diverse group" of academics involved in the grain industry supported the CBOT plan, saying it would not affect Toledo-area producers and meets the statutory rules. --"By any measurement, CBOT's proposed delivery system provides more deliverable supply than the current system," he said. --Donovan said ownership of eligible elevators along the Illinois River was dispersed and the number of barge-loading facilities sufficient with the proposed new system. The rate of concentration of elevator ownership under the new plan was less than under the current system, which allows for delivery in Chicago, Toledo, St Louis and Burns Harbor, Indiana, he said. There were 11,535 jumbo covered barges owned by 49 firms on the northern Illinois River in 1996, compared with three firms owning 75 percent of the vessels transporting grain on the Great Lakes, Donovan said.

Brooksley Born, head of the CFTC, told Reuters on June 26 that a decision on the CBOT's proposal could be expected in the next month or two. CBOT chairman Patrick Arbor said two weeks ago that the exchange would go to court if necessary if the agency rejected the plan, which has been attacked in many of the 650 formal comments CFTC has received.
